issues.explanation: The trigger set is not clinically coherent for this trauma profile. As a male firefighter whose index trauma is relief work in a war zone, moral-violation cues are plausible, but 'Babies' and especially 'Comments on sexual violence' imply highly specific trauma-linked content that is not supported anywhere else in the memory, threat, or appraisal items. Those other nodes describe moral injury, disorganized trauma memory, pain recall, anger, and global alienation, but contain no infant-related or sexual-violence-related material. This makes those two triggers feel disconnected from the rest of the formulation rather than part of the same trauma network.

issues.explanation: Within Maladaptive Strategies, 'Avoid Feelings' is internally contradictory in wording: 'Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion' describes the opposite of emotional avoidance. It conflicts with the node label and with the rest of the profile, which otherwise suggests suppression/avoidance and control strategies in response to distress. This item is therefore not clinically coherent as selected.

issues.item: Avoid Feelings: Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion
issues.explanation: This item directly contradicts the Maladaptive Strategies construct and the rest of the profile. 'Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion' describes openness to emotion rather than avoidance of feelings. It is internally inconsistent within the node, where the other items are clearly maladaptive avoidance/control strategies (self-harm to regulate affect, mental rituals to prevent recurrence), and it does not fit the cognitive formulation linking negative appraisals, memory, and threat to maladaptive coping.

vignette:
Ravi had spent most of his adult life as a firefighter in a large American city, but the event that later defined his treatment had taken place years earlier, when he was deployed as a relief worker in a war zone after shelling had torn through a residential district. One afternoon, while helping pull survivors from a collapsed building, an explosion went off nearby with a force that seemed to shake the street itself. In the confusion he heard men shouting, then the sudden silence that followed, and he saw the aftermath of violence that made ordinary rules feel useless. What he has never been able to fully settle in his mind is his own role in those hours; he came away feeling that he had acted in ways that went against who he was. That conviction settled quickly into the belief that his life had been destroyed by the trauma and that he no longer belonged anywhere, not with the local families he had tried to help, and not later among the people back home who could not understand what he had seen.

In the months that followed, Ravi began to react sharply to anything that resembled the war zone in miniature. A bang from a dumpster lid slamming in the station bay, a mortar-like backfire on the street, or even a sudden pop from a construction site could bring the event back with frightening force. At those moments, the memory did not return as a clean story but as fragments he could not put in the right order: the wall buckling, someone crying, his own hands moving before he could think. He could not find words to describe what had happened, and when the memory came on, he felt physical pain in the same parts of his body as during the event, as if the strain had been stored there. The same was true when he encountered comments about sexual violence on the news or heard someone making light of people’s suffering, or when he watched people misbehaving in ways that struck him as cruel or reckless; those moments reopened the same scene and made him feel that the world was again full of danger and disgrace. Each reminder fed his sense that he had crossed a moral line and that his life had been irreparably altered, and he began to read even ordinary encounters through that lens, seeing himself as cut off from others and permanently marked.

Those appraisals soon shaped his attempts to get through the day. Ravi would try hard not to think about the trauma, forcing himself away from any image or thought that might surface. When the feelings became too strong, he sometimes hurt himself physically just enough to release the overwhelming pressure, later describing it as the only thing that made the inner noise stop for a moment. He also performed private mental rituals, repeating phrases and checks in his head to prevent bad things from happening again, as though enough precision might keep the past from returning. Yet these efforts never stayed contained. The more he tried to suppress the memories, the more they seemed to slip back in, jagged and incomplete, and the more his body registered them as pain. In turn, the return of those fragments made him feel more threatened, more ashamed, and more certain that he was not safe in his own mind. His fear and shame made him even more determined to control his thoughts, and that control only kept the event alive.

Over time Ravi also became increasingly on guard. Strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, and shame came on quickly, and he became irritable, snapping at people at work and at home, sometimes with an aggression that left him embarrassed afterward. Unusual silence was especially hard for him; if a room went quiet, he felt something dangerous was about to happen, as if the stillness itself were the prelude to another blast or another deadening loss. Those states of alarm made his belief that he had ruined his life feel even more convincing, and they sharpened his sense that he belonged nowhere. They also pushed him back toward the same attempts to manage himself through silence, suppression, ritual, and, at the worst moments, self-harm. Because he expected danger and felt so contaminated by what he remembered, he became more sensitive to every potential cue: every bang near the firehouse, every cruel remark on television, every sign of moral failure in other people.

Ravi’s work and daily life had slowly contracted around these reactions. At the station he could not relax when the apparatus floor went quiet, and at home after his divorce he found himself alone with the very thoughts he most wanted to avoid. He finally came for help when his irritability and physical self-injury began to frighten him, and when he realized that the rituals and suppression were taking more from him than they were protecting. What he wants most now is to stop feeling that he is still back in that war zone, and what he fears most is that if the memories break through again, they will prove that he has already become someone he does not recognize.
